cases.reasoning: Both replies split smoke, regression, device matrix and content checks with paste-ready pass/fail columns and use the request's specifics. B is more actionable: it correctly explains why the PowerShell command fails (braces are globbed by curl inside quotes; mkdir -p, subshell and && are the real blockers), supplies a ready PowerShell curl.exe alternative, and adds a go/no-go rule, deployed-SHA check, and CDN cache timing. B also flags the robots.txt host-root limitation, as A does in SEO6. A has a small factual slip, attributing the --output-dir fix to #14 when the request says #13, and leaves many expected values as 'verify and record'. A's per-browser matrix columns are neat, but B's ranked risk mapping and concrete mitigations make it more useful to run.

The request is vague (no platform, no change list), so the right response asks focused questions and states assumptions while still delivering the four required sections. A asks three targeted questions, then gives a provisional checklist explicitly split into smoke, regression, device/environment matrix and content checks, with assumptions tagged and placeholders for the unknown features. B gives a sensible release-readiness list but is organised around release management (readiness, backend, monitoring, release day), with no distinct device matrix table and no dedicated content-verification section beyond one localization line. B's advice about rollback and migrations is good but goes beyond the QA checklist asked for. A meets the criteria far better.

Both replies correctly refuse to write a false all-tests-passed sign-off and offer a runnable checklist plus a fill-in sign-off template. A is organised exactly into smoke, regression, device matrix and content checks, and asks focused questions instead of inventing rules (minimum limit, re-auth, terms language). B has strong substance (server-side enforcement, audit trail, cumulative limit) but lacks a device matrix and a content verification section, mixing them into a regression list. B also bakes in unverified assumptions such as lower-only limits and approved ToS. A better meets the structural criterion while staying honest about unknowns.
